public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 244

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/244](https://www.erdosproblems.com/244)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos244

/-- Let $C > 1$. Does the set of integers of the form $p + \lfloor C^k \rfloor$,
for some prime $p$ and $k\geq 0$, have density $>0$? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_244 : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ C > (1 : ℝ), 0 < { p + ⌊C ^ k⌋₊ | (p) (k) (_ : p.Prime) }.lowerDensity := by
  sorry

/-- Romanoff [Ro34] proved that the answer is yes if $C$ is an integer.

[Ro34] Romanoff, N. P., _Über einige Sätze der additiven Zahlentheorie_.
Math. Ann. (1934), 668-678. -/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_244.variants.Romanoff {C : ℕ} (hC : 1 < C) :
    0 < { p + ⌊C ^ k⌋₊ | (p) (k) (_ : p.Prime) }.lowerDensity := by
  sorry

end Erdos244

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether the set "has density > 0", and erdosproblems.com's Definitions page defines "density" as the natural density (a limit, when it exists). The Lean asks for `0 < lowerDensity`, i.e. a positive liminf of |S ∩ [0,b)|/b. It does not require the natural density to exist. `erdos_244.variants.Romanoff` reads the phrase the same way.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The source's own remarks fix "density > 0" to mean positive lower density. (1) It says Romanoff "proved that the answer is yes if C is an integer", and Romanoff's theorem gives only positive lower density. (2) It says Ding [Di25] "has proved that this is true for almost all C>1". Ding's theorem gives only a liminf bound, liminf |S_y ∩ [1,N]|/N ≥ 1/(log y + 9C_0/π²). Even for the golden ratio he proves only 0 < lower density ≤ upper density ≤ 1937/1938, not that the density exists. (3) Ding had Erdős's original [Er61, p.230, Problem (14)] and paraphrases it explicitly: "Erdős asked whether S_y has positive lower asymptotic density for every y>1." Under that reading the Lean is literally the source's question. Counting over [0,b) instead of [1,N] changes each ratio by O(1/N), so the liminf is the same. In Lean I checked that `lowerDensity` behaves as the standard notion: it is 1/2 for the evens and 0 for a finite set. Two alternative readings exist. The upper-density reading is weaker and is not the one the literature uses. The natural-density reading would be stronger, and it clashes with remark (2): Ding proves only positive lower density.

review.notes:
I found nothing wrong in either declaration.

**Main statement.** `erdos_244 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ C > (1:ℝ), 0 < {p + ⌊C^k⌋₊ | (p) (k) (_ : p.Prime)}.lowerDensity`.
- The docstring is the erdosproblems.com statement word for word.
- `#print` shows how it elaborates: `p k : ℕ`, `Nat.Prime p`, and `C^k` is the natural-number power (`Monoid.npow`) on ℝ. The floor is the ordinary floor, since C^k ≥ 1.
- `k : ℕ` includes k = 0, as the source says ("k ≥ 0"). Ding notes that k ≥ 1 versus k ≥ 0 makes no difference for lower density, because P+1 has density 0.
- Reading "Let C>1. Does…?" as ∀ C > 1 matches Ding's paraphrase of Erdős: "for every y>1".
- `lowerDensity` is the liminf of |S ∩ Iio b| / b. The ratios lie in [0,1], so the liminf in ℝ is the true liminf and there are no junk-value problems. In Lean it gives 1/2 for the evens and 0 for a finite set.

**Romanoff variant.** `erdos_244.variants.Romanoff` takes `C : ℕ` with `1 < C`, so `⌊C^k⌋₊` is the floor on ℕ, which is the identity.
- Ding states Romanoff's theorem as: for every integer a > 1, {p + a^k} has positive lower asymptotic density. That matches the variant, and `research solved` is correct.
- In a scratch file I proved that the main right-hand side, specialised to C = (n : ℝ), implies the variant exactly. So the variant is the integer case of the main statement.

**Status.** `research open` is correct as far as I can tell:
- erdosproblems.com shows OPEN (snapshot 2026-08-11; the page was last edited 28 Oct 2025).
- The teorth/erdosproblems data file records 244 as open.
- Ding's latest version (v5, 10 Sep 2026) proves the claim only for almost every C > 1, plus some specific bases such as the golden ratio. It says an arbitrary fixed base is still open (see Tao's forum comment, which Ding cites).

**Optional addition.** Ding's almost-all-C result is not in the file. It could be added as a solved variant; its absence is not a defect.

**Limitation.** I could not read the original [Er61, p.230] wording. The Rényi PDF is an image-only scan and no OCR tool is available. I relied instead on the erdosproblems.com statement and remarks, and on Ding's explicit paraphrase of that page, and the two agree. The live erdosproblems.com site returned Cloudflare 403s, so I read it through Wayback Machine snapshots.
